speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I wish to take this opportunity to express my heartfelt thanks to all our healthcare workers for the tireless work they have been doing for us all these years and, in particular, during this pandemic.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: It has not been easy, but we have been very appreciative of all that they have done.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Hence, any help for these families is welcomed and much appreciated.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Through a $3-to-$1 matching donation from the Government to the RDF, it is with the hope that this would encourage the larger community including philanthropists, corporates, community groups and individuals to join in to support these patients in fostering a more caring and inclusive society.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In just five months after the introduction of RDF, the initial fund of $70 million has increased to $90 million.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: However, a year since November 2019, it was reported by MOH that the value of the RDF had only increased from $90 million to $93 million, with one's hypothesis that a comparatively slower increase could be due to the economic fall-out from COVID-19, which saw a corresponding decrease in public donations.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While I understand that the objective of the RDF is to sustainably support beneficiaries, giving them the assurance that financial support will be available over their lifetime, but the number of beneficiaries since the introduction of the RDF appears to be small.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Today's Motion seeks to explore ways to increase the uptake of the RDF through more awareness, expanding the scope of eligible conditions and drugs under the RDF.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Further, what can be done to ensure sustainability of the RDF through continued encouragement of donation and the involvement of medical insurers and drug manufacturers?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In response to a Parliamentary Question by Dr Tan Wu Meng, MOH replied that, currently, only six medicines that treat the four rare conditions are eligible for the RDF, with a few more drugs under consideration.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While I can understand the RDF had, indeed, managed to assist seven beneficiaries, I cannot help but worry about the other 2,000 Singaporeans with rare diseases and how they are being supported.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Thus, I would like to raise some points for MOH to consider.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: First, potential to increase the uptake of the RDF.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: With only eight applications received since the introduction of the RDF, it begs the question, are we doing enough through the RDF?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: There are possibly reasons why people do not apply: from not fulfilling the eligibility requirements, to other funding sources available, lack of awareness of the existence of the RDF, or some reasons we may not even be aware of.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Regarding the eligibility requirements, I would call for an expansion in scope in the list of drugs and conditions eligible for the RDF.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: But before that, the question is, are there sufficient awareness on the existence of the RDF amongst those who are suffering from rare diseases?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I understand that groups like the Rare Disorders Society (Singapore) and Rainbow Across Borders help in raising awareness and providing support to patients with rare diseases.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: But could there be further touchpoints that could allow those with rare diseases to know more about and benefit from the RDF?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: For example, this could be more widely shared through the community level and family touchpoints like the general practitioners, pediatricians and polyclinics.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Second, the list of conditions that are eligible for the RDF.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: For the current four eligible conditions for the RDF, there is a strict process in assessing eligibility.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Understandably so, as we want to ensure that those who really need the funds can obtain the funds and on a long-term basis.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: However, for those with rare diseases beyond these four eligible conditions, they face the strictest of processes and a flat rejection.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: One example would be the Ding family whose young daughter suffers from Turner Syndrome, a condition, currently, that is not eligible and, despite their best efforts in appealing for coverage, they were rejected.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: There are, presently, over 6,000 types of rare diseases in the world and, yet, only four types are eligible for the RDF.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While I can understand that it is not feasible to be comprehensive and exhaustive to cover all rare diseases for eligibility, could we do more to expand the current scope of conditions?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The sad truth is that some of these rare diseases that affect young children currently do not have any treatments that are readily available and, even if they do have some form of preventive measures, the measures would, usually, result in death.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Hence, it is very important that for conditions with appropriate treatments and medications, we provide sufficient resources and support to ensure that these young children who need it, get it.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: With that, I would like to propose to include coverage of the following two conditions: neuroblastoma and Krabbe Disease.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: These two conditions have been listed under the 10 most common rare diseases among young children in the world today.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Neuroblastoma is one of the most common childhood cancers found in children under the age of five.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The younger the disease develops in the individual, the more severe it would be as they grow to adulthood.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Third, the list of drugs that are eligible for the RDF.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: With reference to the United States, there are close to 30 million people who suffer from some form of rare disease.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved 22 novel drugs in 2019 alone just to combat against a variety of rare diseases.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While it is understood that the RDF is currently considering more drugs for eligibility, could the Minister shed more light on the process and timeline of the type of drugs under evaluation?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In order to expedite approval and eligibility to allow more beneficiaries for this fund, could there be an opportunity for the RDF to collaborate with overseas governments and institutions to exchange research and information?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This will better accelerate local understanding of different rare diseases and the corresponding drugs and treatments here.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Current eligibility for drugs under the RDF follows a rigorous process.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I am not against a rigorous process, as, rightfully so, this matters lives.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: But could some relaxation on the criteria for drug approval be exercised to include palliative care as well?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: For the Krabbe Disease, there are, currently, no cures with the existing treatments.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: What is available, usually, involves the relief of the severity of the symptoms as well as supportive care.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Only a limited number of success in infants who were given stem cell transplants at an early age had been known at this stage.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: For the 43 Singaporeans with Krabbe Disease, they have to shoulder the high medical costs year after year.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: If the drug eligibility could be relaxed, I believe this would bring some respite and cheer to them and help them to continue life with zest despite the perennial looming thought that the disease has no cure and the treatment can only allay their symptoms.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Looking at our nation with an ageing population and the likely exponential budgets we are projecting for future healthcare costs, I can only imagine the treatment costs for rare diseases and, consequently, the RDF as no exception.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The following two points would explore how to ensure the sustainability of the RDF and the role of medical insurance and drug manufacturers in achieving this goal together.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: So, first, the efficacy and sustainability of the RDF.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: However, with the call to increase the scope of conditions and drugs included, it is inevitable this will lead to more funds required if the number of beneficiaries grows.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Herein lies the question: how do we ensure sustainability of the RDF, so that the RDF would be able to last the beneficiaries a lifetime and also account for an increase in the number of recipients?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: As last year has shown, community donations are very much dependent on economic conditions.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: However, those suffering from rare diseases cannot stop treatment and wait for the conditions to improve, regardless of economic conditions.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: So, how can we encourage a more sustainable and recurring model of community donations?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Besides raising awareness on the RDF for more fundraising efforts, can corporate donations that span over a period of five to 10 years be explored with differentiated tax treatment?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In so doing, it could increase donations from corporates or family offices.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: With some certainty in donations, it could help to act as a bulwark against the smaller community donations that are more dependent and fluctuate according to economic conditions.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Given the limited drugs that are available for each rare disease, the drug manufacturers can consider, as their social effort, to pay it forward and balancing the cost offset with other commercial drugs in their portfolio by subsidising the cost of trial or unique medication, or what they call "novel drugs" for patients.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This will greatly assist the patients as they are restricted by options, to begin with, and unable to bear the cost of standard commercial models of drugs and treatment.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: So, this is probably a critical way forward for a sustainable outcome.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The pricing of insurance premiums is a delicate one.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Through a risk-pooling mechanism, insurers seek to diversify the risk of payout.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Generally, in recent times, insurance premiums have been increasing, with increased consumption of medical services as an oft-cited reason.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While active measures have been taken to keep the insurance premiums in check, this will place an even heavier toll on those with rare diseases; if only they are covered in the first place.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Having medical insurance does, indeed, help take some financial and mental pressure off the individual and their family.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This may allow them to better focus on improving and have better health outcomes.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: But as a country, it is pivotal that we try our utmost to support them through the RDF and other means and jointly work towards our vision of creating a more caring and inclusive society.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I look forward to the Senior Minister of State's reply.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In addition to the suffering that the child goes through, it also creates a lot of emotional distress, uncertainties and anxieties for the parents and can impose greater financial as well as physical demands in caring for the needs of the child.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The high cost of treatment adds to the overall burden.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As a doctor, I have walked this difficult journey with many patients and their families before, especially when they had an unexpected diagnosis being revealed to them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: So, I would like to thank Miss Cheryl Chan for her passionate speech and proposals relating to the Rare Disease Fund (RDF) in support of these families.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The RDF supports high-cost, life-saving treatments for very rare genetic conditions where the medicines, firstly, have a proven therapeutic efficacy; secondly, are able to substantially extend a patient's lifespan and maintain a quality of life as a direct consequence of its use and; thirdly, be reasonably priced as when compared to its price in other countries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Rare diseases with onset in childhood are prioritised initially as these patients with conditions, such as rare diseases, can often go on to lead full and meaningful lives if they are diagnosed early in the course of their disease and receive the required treatment promptly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Because these treatments tend to be lifelong, the RDF is structured as an endowment fund to ensure that only the interest income generated is used to fund the treatment and the capital sum continues to generate a sustainable stream of income to ensure patients enrolled into the programme will have assured support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: While welcoming the set-up of the RDF, Miss Cheryl Chan has highlighted that the number of patients, conditions and medicines covered by the RDF is low, potentially leaving some rare diseases patients unassisted.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: First, this is not a situation in which eligible patients are not applying for the RDF due to a lack of awareness.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In fact, as the costs are high, patients with rare diseases, generally, seek care in the public sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We can, therefore, easily identify patients with rare diseases covered by the RDF and invite those who require financial assistance to apply.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Furthermore, many of the public sector specialists who treat genetic disorders are on the expert panel that advises the RDF Committee on the rare disease medicines that should be considered for coverage by the RDF.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Some patients with rare diseases have insurance coverage or alternative financial means and need not apply for RDF grants.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For those who are in financial need, medical social workers in the public healthcare institution and the patient’s specialist will assist the patient to apply for RDF assistance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Second, when we first set up the RDF, it was established that there were up to 2,000 patients with rare diseases in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: However, the majority of these patients have conditions where no treatments are available to correct the genetic deficiency and life expectancy may be limited with poor quality of life; or where treatments were relatively low cost and, hence, can already be supported under current funding sources.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We had, therefore, anticipated there could be up to 15 medicines that needed RDF support, based on experiences of equivalent rare disease funds from overseas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We need to do more, but it is tangible progress in a short time of two years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Third, Miss Cheryl Chan also proposed to list more rare diseases and medicines on the RDF.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We should only do so if the rare diseases have effective treatments that can meaningfully extend the life expectancy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But adding more medicines does not, in itself, enable more patients to be helped, especially if the RDF does not have sufficient funds to support more patients for the entire lifetime of their treatment costs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: They will grow and increase in body weight, which means that the medication dosage required, along with the cost of treatment, will go up commensurately.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In the coming years, the annual sum in grant payouts required would increase significantly just to support these same patients.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We have to cater for these increases with age when we decide how many patients the RDF can sustain, in order that the supported patients can be assured that they can continue to afford their medications once they are started on treatment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The reality is that this is a large sum for a very small number of patients.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But that is how expensive rare diseases medicine costs and why we need all of us – the Government, the community – to work together to help this group.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Without more donations, it will be very difficult for the RDF to list more medicines or to support new patients.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This, therefore, brings me to the crux of what will allow RDF to help more patients with rare diseases – raising more donations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Miss Cheryl Chan has also recognised this in her speech.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This also applies to all donations made by corporations and family offices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Fully aware of the importance of raising more funds, the RDF Committee, together with its secretariat at KK Hospital, is doubling up their efforts to raise funds.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: It has and will continue to approach high networth individuals, foundations as well as corporate sponsors, as suggested by Miss Cheryl Chan.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: It also stands ready to collaborate with organisations to help raise funds for the RDF, as it has done so on a few occasions in the past.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: It is also exploring how it can develop a base of supporters who can reach out to their networks to fundraise.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The RDF Committee will appreciate all the help that it can get.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: If Members of this House would like to help raise funds for the RDF, please let me know and I will gladly put you in touch with the RDF Committee.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: First, Miss Cheryl Chan proposed to include two specific rare diseases: neuroblastoma and Krabbe Disease.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Treatments for cancer, including neuroblastoma, are not covered under the RDF as mainstream financing is available through MediShield Life currently.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Those who need further assistance can apply for MediFund.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As for Krabbe Disease, there are, unfortunately, no treatments available to slow disease progression today, with most patients succumbing by age two.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The current available medicines are for palliative and supportive care only, which would not fulfil the inclusion criteria for RDF of being able to substantially extend a patient’s lifespan.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Patients who require additional assistance for palliative care are already supported via mainstream financing schemes, such as subsidies and our 3M of MediSave, MediShield Life and MediFund.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Miss Cheryl Chan also suggested going beyond the RDF and leveraging more on insurance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I note that Miss Cheryl Chan is familiar with the practice among private insurers of not covering pre-existing illnesses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Where coverage of pre-existing illnesses is provided, it comes with the loading of the insurance premium, which can be significant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The benefits and premiums of private insurance products, such as Integrated Shield Plans (IPs), are determined by insurers, based on their own commercial and actuarial considerations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In doing so, insurers have to strike a balance between providing more comprehensive coverage and ensuring the affordability of premiums, as well as the sustainability of their insurance fund.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As private insurance is optional, the insurers also need to guard against adverse selection that can affect sustainability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Miss Cheryl Chan may, however, be pleased to know that some insurance products, such as IPs, do not set exclusions for rare diseases, unless these are pre-existing conditions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Where there are claims limits to payouts such that there remains an out-of-pocket payment for the patient, the RDF would consider an application to support this remaining out-of-pocket payment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The task remains ahead of us, as a community, to muster all the necessary resources and assistance that we all agree are needed for this group of fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I encourage everyone to donate generously, so that more can benefit from the RDF.
